summary: Registers a URN namespace for the European Broadcasting Union to name persistent resources in its technical documentation and Internet resources, such as specifications, XML schemas, classification schemes, namespaces, style sheets and media assets. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Broadcasters have many documents and files. This paper gives them an official name style so every item has a permanent name that does not change.

questions: how does the ebu name resources
subtitle: A standard namespace for naming EBU resources and documents.

tldr.problem: The European Broadcasting Union produces many technical resources, specifications, XML schemas, and classification schemes that need persistent, location-independent names for identification and cross-reference across systems.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5174 registers a formal URN namespace called 'ebu' with the IANA, allowing the EBU to assign unique, hierarchical identifiers using the pattern urn:ebu:{category}:{string}.
tldr.outcome: The namespace provides a stable way to identify EBU resources, enabling interoperability with other systems and specifications that incorporate or reference EBU technical materials.

today: RFC 5174 remains in effect as the registration of the urn:ebu namespace. It is Informational and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What the EBU Is and Why It Needs Persistent Names
sections.content:
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) is the world's largest non-profit professional association of broadcasters, founded in 1950 with more than 70 active members in 55 countries. It negotiates broadcasting rights for major sports events, operates Eurovision and Euroradio, organizes program exchanges and co-productions, and provides technical advice and standardized solutions across broadcast systems.

As the EBU develops new delivery methods—especially over the Internet and IP-based networks—it produces a growing number of technical resources: specifications, XML schemas, classification schemes, metadata definitions, and style sheets. These resources are often incorporated or referenced by other organizations' systems. To ensure these resources can be reliably identified and located regardless of where they move or how they are accessed, the EBU needed a formal, persistent naming system.
sections.plainLanguage: The EBU is a big organization that makes lots of technical documents and standards for broadcasters. They needed a system where each document gets an official permanent name so people can always find it, no matter where it is stored.

sections.title: The URN Namespace Structure
sections.content:
RFC 5174 registers the urn:ebu namespace with the IANA (Internet Assigned Numbers Authority). A URN is a Uniform Resource Name—a way to identify a resource by what it is, rather than where it lives (unlike a URL).

All EBU URNs follow a hierarchical structure: urn:ebu:{category}:{string}. The category field is case-insensitive and organizes resources by type (such as 'metadata', 'metadata-cs', or others defined by the EBU). The string portion is case-sensitive and uniquely identifies the specific resource within that category. For example, urn:ebu:metadata:pmeta_2007 identifies a particular metadata document.

The EBU maintains strict control over URN assignment through its metadata expert group under the Production Management Committee, ensuring each URN is unique and never reassigned.
sections.plainLanguage: All EBU names follow the pattern urn:ebu:[type]:[name]. The type tells you what kind of thing it is (like metadata or classification), and the name is the specific document. Each one is unique and permanent.

sections.title: Resources and Categories
sections.content:
The urn:ebu namespace identifies a wide range of resources produced and managed by the EBU. These include XML schema definition files that define the structure of broadcast metadata documents, classification schemes that organize content by type or category, and identification systems that track broadcast assets and content.

The namespace also covers style sheets, namespaces, XML DTDs (Document Type Definitions), and other technical definitions used in broadcast and IP-based delivery. The EBU assigns categories hierarchically based on its organizational structure, allowing for organized growth as new resource types are created.

Each category can support multiple resources, and the EBU ensures that communities using EBU specifications or incorporating EBU resources can rely on these permanent identifiers for versioning, interoperability, and long-term reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The namespace covers all the different kinds of documents and standards the EBU makes: definitions of how documents should be structured, lists of categories for organizing content, rules for naming things, and more. Each type of thing gets its own category name.

sections.title: Resolution and Management
sections.content:
The EBU maintains URN catalogues that map each assigned URN to specific Uniform Resource Locators (URLs). These catalogues enable web-based resolution of named resources—when someone encounters a URN like urn:ebu:metadata:pmeta_2007, the catalogue provides the actual location where that resource can be retrieved.

Validation of URNs is performed by checking them against the maintained catalogues and by verifying they conform to syntax rules specific to each category. The EBU has published its technical activities and metadata information at http://www.ebu.ch/metadata.

Although the RFC was published in 2008, the document notes that future interactive online resolution systems may be developed to automate URI resolution. In the meantime, static catalogues serve as the primary resolution mechanism, and the EBU may authorize additional resolution services as appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: The EBU keeps a big index that says which urn:ebu name points to which actual file or web page. When you see a URN, you can look it up in their index to find where the actual document is stored.

sections.title: Community Adoption and Uses
sections.content:
The RFC identifies three main groups who benefit from the urn:ebu namespace. Implementers and users of EBU resources can now refer to EBU specifications with stable, global identifiers that gain the benefits of Internet-wide interoperability. Implementers of other specifications that incorporate or build upon EBU resources can use URNs to reference and enhance other specifications while maintaining interoperability. Creators of semantically related specifications—such as metadata frameworks and ontology systems—can use EBU resource identifiers to enable interoperation across specification communities.

The value of the namespace is particularly important as new IP-based delivery media (like the Internet and mobile networks), web services, search engines, and semantic web technologies become central to broadcast distribution. With persistent URN identifiers, resources can be reliably located, versioned, and referenced across heterogeneous systems and organizations.
sections.plainLanguage: Broadcasters, software companies, and other organizations can now use these permanent names in their own systems and documents, knowing the names will never change. If someone builds a new system that uses EBU definitions, they can point to them by their permanent URN names.
